Under these circumstances I think we should carefully consider whether or not we may not be enacting legislation which looks upon the face of it to be excellent, but which has imposed upon it the condition of a guarantee by a province and a municipality, and which may become abortive, and which would be absolutely useless from the standpoint of practical application until the legislatures met.
And what is more, I think I should say to the minister that in some of the provinces I know the municipalities have no power of guaranteeing unless they get the exact, specific legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: No power to borrow.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: No power to guarantee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
They do not guarantee
nothing; the municipality does not guarantee.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: I thought it was proposed that a municipality should give its guarantee for the payment of debentures, where they were issued on self-liquidating schemes by boards owned by the municipality, which, however, would guarantee the payment of debentures issued by the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
That of course would
come in in that sense.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Yes; because the minister gave an illustration, and I thought I followed him accurately.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
But that is a rare case.
In most cases they are owned directly.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
Yes, but in one or two
instances of which the Minister of Finance has knowledge, they did set up by statute an independent body for the purpose of operating their utility; and as I followed his illustration it would be possible for this legislation to be made available to them, provided the city gave its guarantee as being the

Municipal Improvements
real owner of the utility, although the debentures would be the debentures not of the municipality but of the utility.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: The municipality would never have to obtain authorization from the province.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
Yes, that is the point I make. Those are the two points I think we shall have to consider carefully when we come to the bill itself. For frankly I do not see how we are going to make this effective without the legislatures of the provinces taking steps to give their guarantees, or to authorize such guarantees to be given. I am not interposing this in any way as an obstruction, but rather as a suggestion which I think will have to be met before we can this year make it effective. The Minister of Labour has indicated how desirable it is that we should do so. That difficulty could be overcome in part by making the distribution a matter as between the provinces and the municipalities, provided the provinces would have the power they have heretofore enjoyed in that regard.
But a look at the orders in council downstairs does not induce one to believe that self-liquidation has been the sole determining factor in the granting of the aid to which reference has been made. Under the circumstances I think we will have to give the utmost consideration to the details of the measure. The minister has said that the resolution is as detailed as he thought he could make it. There are some details he has supplied in his very admirable explanation, but I am afraid that unless we go beyond the terms of the resolution, or if we follow strictly the terms of the resolution, we will find we have placed upon the statute book an act that provides for something being done next year, after the legislatures of the provinces have met and authorized their several governments to give the guarantees which, under the resolution, constitute an essential feature of the proposal.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Would the right hon. member permit a remark?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: It occurs to me that in many legislatures statutes were passed concerning unemployment and relief acts. I am sure that in Quebec similar legislation was passed, stipulating that it was for unemployment or relief, and the municipality was not bound to obtain authorization from the province. Otherwise it would be necessary to have either a referendum or the authorization of the provincial government.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: What the hon. member has said is correct so far as the municipalities are concerned. But the point I was endeavouring to make was that unless and until the legislatures of the several provinces have authorized their governments to give guarantees for the repayment of the sums advanced by the dominion under this legislation, it cannot become workable under the terms of the resolution now before us. I think there is no doubt as to that, and as many of the legislatures have risen for the year 1938 it will be essential for us to consider, when the bill based on this resolution is before us, whether we are in a position to insist upon that guarantee being given. It would involve the minister ascertaining from the several provinces whether or not they have the authority to give the guarantees without further legislation.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: The same difficulty will occur even if the distribution is made to the provinces.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: No, because some of them have power to give promises to pay, which would be the same thing with respect to unemployment relief as a guarantee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
Perhaps I should at this stage indicate what is in the mind of the government regarding the point raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). Xn fact, I think I should apologize for not having anticipated it, but I overlooked it completely in making my statement.
The laws of the provinces relating to municipal expenditures vary very widely; the powers vested by the legislatures in the various lieutenant governors in council vary very widely as also do the powers extended to municipalities to do certain things involving capital expenditure. It is quite impossible to frame a measure which would meet all the varying conditions, and I was compelled therefore to visualize the possibility that this scheme might have a sufficient appeal to the various provincial authorities to warrant them even in calling the legislature together for a couple of days to make possible what might be required in their particular case, for the municipalities on the one hand and for themselves on the other, to enable them to come within the ambit of the legislation.
I will be perfectly frank, Mr. Chairman, and say that I do not think the dominion can extend this credit on any less secured terms than those involved in the bill. As the one charged with the guardianship of the treasury, I should say that I believe the security asked for by this legislation is reasonable and no more than adequate so far as

Municipal Improvements

the dominion is concerned, especially when we have in mind the fact that each legislature controls absolutely the municipalities within its borders. The municipalities are wholly the creatures at all times of the provincial legislatures. If we proceed to lend direct to the municipalities-and there is some question whether we could, as indicated by the leader of the opposition,-it would be open to any provincial legislature so to change the conditions under which its municipalities operate as to make it quite impossible for us to get the money back. We might as well face that. That being the case, seeing that we are rendering this assistance to institutions which are wholly the creatures of provincial legislatures, I think that when we are lending the money so cheaply, when we are taking the degree of loss on the loan which I indicated in my earlier remarks on the subject, the minimum security we should ask is that the province should guarantee that the municipality will keep the obligation it has incurred for a project; and remember, that the project must itself have the approval of the provincial government before it can become eligible for a loan under this statute.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: And be self-liquidating.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: And be self-liquidating. I would not regard it as a hardship, and I am sure the provinces would not, for the legislatures, if necessary, to meet for the very short time required to enable such amendments to be made to their municipal laws as would enable them to take advantage of this legislation. Before this session is over there may be, there will be, other measures which may involve a similar principle. If we are to extend the credit of this dominion to our various self-governing bodies of one kind or another it seems to me that we must take the constitutional aspect sufficiently into account and that we must receive such security as the people of Canada have the right to expect us to take, especially when the expenditure involves a definite annual contribution by the people of the whole of Canada to the people of a particular part of Canada who are organized into a municipality.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
In view of the earlier remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the remarks now made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), I should like to know specifically, Mr. Chairman, whether in your judgment I am misinterpreting this resolution. I had no idea that I had done so. I instanced a certain municipality in British Columbia which had a

faulty waterworks and desired to improve it; desired to take out the old wooden pipes and replace them with concrete pipes. That is all work which would involve labour, and it would, as I see it, come within the purview and under the provisions of this legislation. Am I correct in so interpreting it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: You have omitted one essential qualification. The work must be self-liquidating.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Oh, yes. That was in my mind, although I did not state it.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: And one other qualification.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: The approval of the provincial government.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: One other.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: It has to provide employment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: That is the essential basis, yes. Might I ask my hon. friend if there is any unemployment in the municipality concerned?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: A great deal? That would be an essential primary condition.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Just to make the resolution unanimous, Mr. Chairman, I wish to endorse it for our group here. I can see that a great deal of credit will be derived from this resolution. I have in mind a problem in Edmonton which for a number of years has been debated, and which has been a financial issue; that is, the addition of another unit to the electric light plant of the city. I assume that would come under this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Provided it comes within the scope of the conditions I have named, yes.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext: Will the minister tell us whether or not the federal government will accept the guarantee of the province of Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF LOANS TO ASSIST MUNICIPALITIES IN MAKING SELF-LIQUIDATING IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:

Does the minister think it is really desirable to say that no proceedings of any kind under this act shall be taken except with the consent of the minister? It deprives the act of its public character and places in the hands of a political official the-administration of justice. That is really what
Radio Broadcasting

it means. It is legislation of a kind that is usually very much frowned upon, for reasons which I think are apparent. If that limitation were confined to certain sections, all right. But to say that all proceedings under the act shall be subject to the approval of the minister is going further than I can recall having been done in any similar situation; because it at once limits the administration of justice, prevents a person who has knowledge from laying a complaint before a justice of the peace, and makes the minister, who is a political officer, the preliminary judge in every case that is adjudicated upon by a magistrate. That is a wrong principle, and I think in practice it was abandoned a long time ago. Under the Lord's Day Act we have special provisions as to proceedings being taken only on the fiat of the attorney general, and it was held in an important case that that fiat had to be signed by the attorney general in person; that his deputy could not do it. The result is that, in a case of the slightest possible violation of the provisions of this very important statute, in a remote section of this country, the minister would have to give his consent, I take it in writing, before proceedings could be taken. I urge upon the minister reconsideration of the application of that very broad principle to this statute; for surely this statute, like all other public statutes, should be capable of enforcement, where there has been open breach, by any citizen laying a complaint before a justice, and proceedings being taken. There are other sections which I admit at once should not be enforced by the average citizen making a complaint, but should be subject entirely to the control of the minister. That would prevent many abuses which might otherwise arise. But I certainly think it is going a very long way to say that any proceedings under a public statute can be taken only with the consent of the minister.

speechtext:
It seems to me the committee is giving very wide powers, almost dictatorial powers, to the Minister of Transport. Under another section he is the sole judge as to what the offences are, and they are to be laid by him. We find that the department in the right of the crown collects all the moneys, and nothing goes to the magistrates or justices of the peace.
We now come to the present section and must consider regulations which have almost force of law behind them. These regulations are made under statutory power given to the minister and his technical officers. How is anyone in Nova Scotia to know that regulations have appeared in the Canada Gazette? The broadcasting legislation is so broad in compass that I say the regulations should be published along with the statutory enactments; because it is now going to be impossible for a person in any part of Canada, whether he be in British Columbia or Nova Scotia, to know what regulations have been passed, or to know that a regulation has been in the Canada Gazette for seven days.
Such person may be guilty under the statute. As has been pointed out to the

minister, we are getting into a new field in which laws are enacted outside the criminal code and outside the powers given in connection with the laying of informations under this measure. Cases are placed in the hands of magistrates or justices of the peace for trial. I think in fairness to the hundreds of thousands of people in Canada who have radios in their homes, they should have greater opportunity of ascertaining what the regulations are. The suggestion of the right hon. the leader of the opposition is along the right lines, but I do not think it goes far enough. The regulations in my opinion should be embodied in the statute. Surely the Minister of Transport and his technical officers are in a position to say what the regulations are going to be and to put them in the statute, so that every one in Canada, no matter where he may live, may know whether or not he is guilty of an infringement of a regulation.
Very few people, with the exception of some in Ottawa, read the Canada Gazette. It is a publication which may go out to members of parliament; but those members are not going to make unpopular suggestions to their constituents; at least I should think they would not. I am asking the minister if there could not be some way in which the regulations would be made clear to the owners of radios, so that advantage would not be taken of them, and so that they would not be accused of being guilty of an offence under regulations of which they had no knowledge? An accused person might say he had no knowledge, and there was no manner in which he could receive it, unless he were a person who read the Canada Gazette.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OP PROVISION RESPECTING PROHIBITED CLASSES

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, May 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Neill for the second reading of Bill No. 112, to amend the Immigration Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OP PROVISION RESPECTING PROHIBITED CLASSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this bill was last before the house I had risen to close the debate. I had intended to be brief; but when I was speaking it occurred to me that in view of the positive and definite statements made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), it would be well for me, not being a lawyer, to check up as to the accuracy of what he said. His statement was to the effect that the passage of this bill would make conditions in British Columbia many times worse than they were before, and would allow thousands and thousands of Japanese to enter provided they possessed the ability to learn English. I took up this matter with every legal expert I could find, and with one accord they said that this was not so. Most of them laughed; some of them swore, and others said, "How could it?" I showed them the Immigration Act and my bill and asked them if it was possible that any increased number of Japanese could come in, and with one accord they said it was impossible.
Section 3 of the Immigration Act contains a number of prohibited classes. People who come under those classes cannot enter Canada under any condition. There are twenty-one different classes set out, and I shall name one or two at random. Persons who are imbeciles, Persons afflicted with tuberculosis, persons who are alcoholics and so on are not allowed in. The twentieth prohibition has to do with people who cannot read any language. I am dealing with the Japanese at the moment, and they would be able to come in if they could read the Japanese language. I add to that prohibition by stating that in addition to any person being able to read their own language, they must be able to read either English, French or some language of Europe. How could that possibly let in more Japanese? They can come in now if they can read their own language. I simply superimpose on that the stipulation that they must be able to read English. Yet we are told that this will allow thousands and thousands of Japanese to come in.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OP PROVISION RESPECTING PROHIBITED CLASSES
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will pardon me, I believe he is wrong there. The number is limited to-day by the gentleman's
Immigration Act

agreement under which so far as Japanese are concerned, the Immigration Act does not apply. If my hon. friend will permit me, I should like to point out that according to his bill, if a Japanese over a certain age can read English, French or any other European language, he would be permitted into the country.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OP PROVISION RESPECTING PROHIBITED CLASSES

subtopic: AMENDMENT OP PROVISION RESPECTING PROHIBITED CLASSES
speechtext:
Never mind. Do not make speeches. It does not matter whose opinion it is. My hon. friend says that they would be allowed to come in if they can speak English, but the gentleman's agreement restricts the number who may come in to 150. My bill does not do away with that restriction. If every Japanese in Japan was able to speak English, the gentleman's agreement would still exist and would permit only 150 to come in. I have the agreement before me; it states that hereafter immigrants from Japan will be subject to all the regulations of the Canadian Immigration Act-the minister evidently did not know that-and then there is the extra provision that the number coming in shall be limited to 150. I repeat that my bill does not repeal the gentleman's agreement that limits the number to 150, so how can thousands and thousands come in? The effect of my bill will be largely to cut down the 150. The classes that come in under the gentleman's agreement are mostly farm labourers and domestic servants, and it is seldom that they can speak anything but Japanese. The restriction imposed by this bill will probably restrict the number coming in to five or perhaps ten a year for some years to come. At most it will be a very small number.
Speaking of labourers reminds me of the interim report made by the committee which was sent out to investigate this matter. I think we should have had an opportunity of seeing that report. I have not seen it, but I believe if it had been presented to this house Bill No. 11 would be the law of the land to-day. I have not the interim report, but I have some of the information that was laid before that committee and I propose to give it to the house. The number of Japanese school children in British Columbia to-day is more than double, 110 per cent to be exact, what it was eleven years ago. The number of Japanese school children in Vancouver to-day is very close to the total number of Japanese school children in British Columbia

eleven years ago. Does this house know that in British Columbia to-day there are 1,000 Japanese on relief? They are not put to the trouble of seizing a public building to get it. They receive their relief as regularly as old age pensions. Yet we have all this quibbling between this government and the British Columbia government about the matter of domicile, and we have the spectacle of white men driven by despair to start what is practically a revolution. It is little better than a revolution even though it is a peaceful one. Yet these Japanese are receiving their relief as regularly as clockwork. These are the facts.
Does the house know that according to the records of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police the deportation of forty-three Japanese was recommended in a given period? Deportation is not recommended unless a crime is committed, and yet these forty-three deportation orders were cancelled at Ottawa. It would appear that the Japanese have some friends at Ottawa. It is generally quite difficult to get a deportation order cancelled. I once tried to get one cancelled in connection with a solitary, lone Scotchman, and I had considerable trouble. Yet these forty-three orders were cancelled even though they had been recommended and appeared on the records of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police,
Here is the final thing. Notice was served on that committee by a Japanese official to the effect that if their investigation resulted in the deportation of not more than ten or fifteen Japanese there would be no serious trouble, but if thirty or forty Japanese were affected then there would be trouble. They were told that there would likely be repercussions in Japan. That was told the committee by a high Japanese official. The picture is this:	When we find men committing
crimes we must not find more than fifteen of them guilty or there will be trouble. It will be just too bad, or else. I believe if these facts had been laid before the house when we were considering Bill No. 11, the vote would have been different.
It is true that this bill does not provide for the total exclusion provided for by Bill No. 11, which should have been passed. The Minister of National Defence approved that bill, but he voted against it. His own national poet says:
He knows the right and doth approve it too,
Condemns the wrong but still the wrong pursues.
The government rejected Bill No. 11 because the Japanese might not like it, but this bill makes no reference to the Japanese by name. They are only one of many of the

Immigration Act
coloured nations of the world which make up three-quarters of the population of the world. The educational test has been in use against the Japanese for many years now,
I think thirty, or at least twenty, as regards Australia and New Zealand.
I object strongly to having it spread on the pages of Hansard and through the radio and the press that I have introduced in this house a bill which would make matters in British Columbia many times worse and allow thousands and thousands of Japanese to come in, when the facts are as I have stated, and they cannot be contradicted. I want to give hon. members a picture of this bill. It reached its second reading in the shape of Bill No. 38. I said what I could in favour of it. There was no objection made against it, no fault found with the matter of it, no comment upon it, no criticism of it. But a point of order was taken in connection with the printing of it, a point of order that has not been enforced for ten years, and had it been enforced impartially that day it would have thrown out nine other bills, six of them important government bills. However, it was thrown out; I brought it in again-the rules allowed it-and it came to the second reading the other night. The whole gamut of technicalities had been exhausted. Believe me, it was gone through with a tooth comb, and it could be attacked only on its merits. There are sixty-three lawyers sitting behind the leader of the government party. The massed intelligence of all that legal ability-for they are able men-would naturally be brought to bear on the subject, and what was the result? The mountain laboured and brought forth, not a mouse; it did not even bring forth the cheese to -bait the mouse. All the concentrated ability of those sixty-three lawyers could produce only this piffle about the thousands and thousands of Japanese. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Taylor) would, I am sure, call it an "emotional argument" which was used in that connection.
That having been disposed of, what is left of the argument against the bill? Nothing, because there were no other arguments put up. There cannot be much wrong with the bill when the only argument used against it is of such a puerile character. But it is going to be condemned. We remember that in the nursery tale we were told that the wolf said he was going to eat Little Red Riding Hood because she had done something against him. When she proved she had not done it, the wolf said, "Well, I am going to eat you because your grandmother did something." When she showed that her grandmother had not done it, the wolf said, "Well,
I am going to eat you, anyhow," and this government is going to kill this bill anyhow, although no argument has been advanced against it. This is not a nursery or a nursery tale; we are a legislative body of lawmakers; we have some privileges and rights, and we ought not to be asked to defeat a bill without some reason being given for doing so. The premier told us, very properly, what in his opinion was wrong with Bill No. 11; but no one on the government side has told us what is wrong with this bill, and yet it is going to be defeated.
If the government will not take the house into its confidence as to the reasons for this course, I am going to take the house into my confidence. I am going to make a diagnosis, as the doctors call it, founded upon the facts as we know them and as they seem to warrant, and suggest the reason why the government is determined to defeat this bill upon a party vote without any justification. The reason is twofold. First, there is nothing wrong with the bill; but, second, there has been an arrangement made with Japan that there will be no further restrictions on immigration for a given period. Not a treaty, of course not; no written agreement; no negotiations even, but just these mysterious diplomatic things they call, I believe, in the highest diplomatic circles, "conversations". If such an arrangement was made, I do not blame the government for living up to it; but I do blame them for making such an important arrangement without consulting this house, which alone has the power to make such an agreement; and still more, having made it, for not having told the house what it was. If that is the explanation, the bargain, not having been sanctioned by us, is not binding on us, and there is no reason why we should yield control over our domestic affairs.

speechtext:
I do not wish the minister to say it. He has had his opportunity. The bill has been up for second reading twice. He had all the time in the world. But I will answer him. I was going to answer him anyway if he had kept quiet. If that is not the explanation, I will furnish another. If he does not like the one horn of the dilemma he can take the other. Is it because the government get political hysterics every time the name of Japan is mentioned? We dare not deal with the strictly domestic matter of our own immigration for fear- and fear is an ugly word, Mr. Speaker-that an alien heathen nation, that has no claim whatever to a grievance, might not like it, a nation whose best claim to fame at the present moment is the fact that it is raping and ravaging a friendly nation whose territory it swore a few short years ago to protect and maintain.
Now, this thing is cumulative. Where is it going to stop? If we yield five per cent of our rights to-day for the sake of peace, six months hence we shall be required to surrender ten per cent, and a year afterwards they will want fifty per cent. Other nations will imitate this policy, and we shall lose their respect.
How did we get their respect? We became a nation, not by the Statute of Westminster that we hear so much about, but through the blood and treasure we spent in France to prevent Canada from becoming a German colony. The Statute of Westminster did something. It gave us power to make our own treaties. A lot of good that did us. If we set our feet on the fatal, bitter path 1 have outlined, soon we shall not be allowed to make our own treaties; we shall not even be allowed to make our own pyjamas, because Japan will discover that she can make them cheaper because of her low standard of living, and they will	be	sent to	Toronto	and soldbelow the cost	of	the raw	material	there. Ifthat is to be our policy, we had better tear up the Statute of Westminster and crawl back as a colony under the overburdened protection of	the	British	nation.	At leastwe would be	safe there;	yes, cheaply safe,
would we not? Britain would give it to us, give it to us to the last exhaustion of her strained powers, and she would not worry and fuss because every now and again we debate whether we would be at war when she is at war. But what a humiliation it would be for us as a nation and as individuals!

Mr. Speaker, it is more than forty-seven years since I came to this country. That is a longer time than the lives of many of the hon. members I see before me. I have married, brought up a family and buried our dead here. I have been a loyal and true Canadian in thought, word and deed. I have taught my children that they must not pay too much attention to the land of their parents, but that they must be true Canadians and bear faithful allegiance to Canada herself. For the first time in nearly half a century I have occasion to be ashamed of my adopted country. To-night we are at the fork of the road. We can say to Japan, "While you have not said you objected to this bill, we have not passed it because we thought you might not like it. We have not exactly cut loose from Britain, but we have indicated that there is no obligation, that there are no commitments if she is in trouble, and to that extent we have weakened her in the eyes of the world; you have our sympathy; we hope you will not be too hard on us." Shall we take that degrading and humiliating position, or shall we say to Japan and to the world, " When Britain is in trouble we are in trouble; when Britain is at war we are at war, and when Britain is in a war, while we cannot bind future parliaments as to the amount of participation, any more than the British parliament is bound, we will do our part; we are solidly behind Great Britain economically, financially and in every other way to the best of our ability." Then, let us say to Japan, "We are determined to run and control our own domestic affairs, of which immigration is one, and another is to decide whether people can be deported or not. That is another privilege and we are going to use it. We are solidly behind the British nation, and the British nation is solidly behind us." That would be the end of it. That would be a policy of courage, a policy of dignity and selfrespect, both for us and from the other nations, and one that would make for the preservation of peace, a bold policy which would put us in standing and reputation with all the nations of the world. Whether we take the short vision of the immediate future or the long vision down the vista of time, it would be a policy that would immediately and ultimately work for the benefit of British Columbia, of Canada and of the British empire in which we are all concerned. I think the first step towards the announcement and the initiation of such a policy would be for us to pass this bill which is before us to-night.

speechtext:
There are so many public hospitals in the county of Jacques Cartier that I consider myself in duty bound to speak on this bill sponsored by the hon. member for Laurier which would permit the holding of sweepstakes under provincial regulations and supervision for the benefit of hospitals and legally constituted universities. No doubt hon. members will be interested to have a list of the hospitals which are in my county. In Lachine we have l'Hopital St. Joseph and the Lachine General Hospital. In Cartierville we have 1'Hopital du Sacre Coeur, better known throughout America as the Hospital for Incurables. At Cote de Neiges we have l'Asile Nazareth, St. Mary's and the Jewish hospital. At St. Laurent there is l'hopital de Notre Dame de l'Esperance.
It is well known that hospitals are having a hard time financially. In all the cities in Canada annual campaigns have to be held to support the hospitals. In many cases that is not sufficient, and provinces and cities have to guarantee their bonds, and not only the bonds but often the interest coupons as well. Therefore there is no doubt about hospitals being in need of financial support. Fortunately there is a large number of anonymous benefactors who help such institutions. Some generous people help them regularly, others at various times or upon special occasions. Some benefactors adopt a certain institution, sometimes because of religious reasons, sometimes because a hospital specializes in the treatment of diseases in which they take an interest. Hospitals devoted to the care of children seem to have a peculiarly strong attraction for good-hearted people, and derive great benefit from their interest. Leading" citizens of both sexes serve on the boards of administration of hospitals and charitable institutions of all kinds. Their services are, of course, given freely; they render them as a duty and often as a hobby as well. They are glad to help their fellow citizens to that extent. This is practical Christianity of a kind of which we are greatly in need. Leading business and professional men deem it an

Mr. Speaker, I desire to express myself in favour of this bill, and I do so because it makes an attempt, although imperfectly, to remove from the criminal code the effort to regulate the moral and ethical expression of our people. I mean by that I am perfectly satisfied that we should control the abuses in our ethical relationships to each other, and in our moralf. as expressed in our economy. But when it comes to regulating and controlling the ordinary expressions of our thoughts, our ideas and our ideals, in ethics and morals, then I contend the criminal code is going altogether too far.
We have had representations from reverend and honourable members claiming that this was really a religious issue. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) brought out a novel interpretation of one of the commandment^, and attempted to make that which was really an ethical instruction a religious teaching. In addition, the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Rowe) made extravagant statements about what would occur in Canada if we permitted this bill to pass. I am not one who believes that the world is necessarily going to the dogs. We are really bettering all the time. Occasionally we have lapses-sometimes by individuals and sometimes in masses. But in the main our progress is forward. And because of that and because I have faith in our people and in ourselves, I am supporting this bill. If it were a question of national ethics, differing entirely from the individual expression, that might have been brought out by some of the speakers to the bill. But I have not discovered that any of them have found that fact.
Holy Writ has been invoked to show us that we would do wrong. But as I look through Holy Writ I cannot discover that it especially teaches us it is wrong to make a stake or to take a gamble. I have a distinct recollection of a celebrated parable:
Behold, a sower went forth to sow;
And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the wayside, and the fowls came and devoured them up:

maintopic: VALIDITY OP QUEBEC STATUTE-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF MR. WOODSWORTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the discussion introduced yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) comes down to a discussion of ideology. It goes deeper than financial or even social matters, and involves principles in which the Canadian nation and also several foreign powers are interested.
It goes still deeper than that. We are compelled in such a discussion to mention internal and domestic policies of foreign nations, although in certain instances nations affected may resent our action. I intend to point out, however, in the few moments at my disposal that the purpose of the discussion is solely in order as forcibly as we can to bring before the house some of the new political philosophies, fallacies and demagogy which have been brought forth in the civilized world in the last fifteen or eighteen years.
In the discussion of the padlock law there is also the matter of internal administration, so far as Quebec is concerned. There is also the matter of morals of which perhaps the people living within the borders of that province are in the best position to judge. They know -best the mentality of their own people.
When we consider the Russian revolution we have to try to analyze the feelings, the inclinations, of the people of that nation.

Validity of Quebec Statute
We have to use metaphor. When we do that we realize that the Russian people are entirely different from Canadians. One of the primary results of that revolution was the decision that brains, intelligence and the faculty to manage and direct were not to be considered as being worth any more than common labour. Of course I realize that in suggesting such a philosophy of internal policy I may be opening up a very wide discussion. There is no doubt that in a democracy labour must of necessity have a primary place in the social functions of the nation. However, we must not forget that the Russian revolutionists practically swept away the intelligentzia of the Russian nation. Any one who possessed a university degree could not take part in the government of that country. There was to be only one class, the proletariat, the workers. I want just to leave this thought with the house to digest. We are all familiar with how soon they found that it was absolutely impossible to carry out these ideas.
Another idea, utterly contrary to western civilization, was that religion should not exist, should be destroyed. They contended that religion of any kind was simply an opiate to civilization. That proletariat government tried to erase religion from that great country. We can easily visualize how repulsive such a policy would be to a civilized Christian country. We must realize how foreign such a policy is to the mentality of Canadian people.
Another idea advanced by the Russian revolutionists was that the individual had no right to any personal gain. The individual lost his identity entirely. The only supreme being was the state under Lenin or Stalin who were practically deified. The individual existed purely and solely for the state. This is another philosophy that is absolutely foreign to Canadians and civilized peoples generally. No doubt this revolution was brought about by injustices suffered by the Russian people under the tzarist regime, but the leaders of that revolution were not content to apply the principles they advocated to Russia alone. To them it was more than a political philosophy; it became almost a religion. We saw the zeal generally connected with any new religion exerted on behalf of this philosophy. In their obsession they were not content to apply their ideas to Russia alone; they wanted to spread them all over the white and coloured world. In a few months after the revolution we saw soviet 51952-217
and bolshevist emissaries in China, India, Japan, Germany, Italy, England, Central America, South America and North America.
An immediate reaction set in in many of these nations when they found these missionaries in their midst. Many of the countries in Europe were still suffering from the results of the great war. The result was that we had the spectacle of communism actually being the parent of fascism and nazism. If communism was not the father of these last two isms, at least it was mainly responsible for the functioning of fascism in Italy and nazism in Germany.
We must be very careful in discussing a matter of this kind. ' We must realize the horizons we have to face. In a discussion of this kind we must visualize the different angles of the situation. You must envisage it within its proper perspective. When you have to deal with a ferocious animal you must take more precaution than when you are dealing with a domestic cat. When you have to dee' with a venomous reptile you must be mov

. careful than when you are handling a songbird. In this case we are dealing with something that is very dangerous, not only to the mentality but to the national life of this country. I well remember only three short years ago when I barely escaped with my life during the bushmen's strike in Cochrane. That strike was instigated by communist leaders, and I say with all the sincerity and knowledge I possess that they were in the pay of soviet Russia. There are some members in the house at the present time, these being known as labour leaders, to whom I went three, four or five years ago and told what had happened. They sympathized with me in my situation because they realized that these communist leaders did not desire a solution of our labour problems. They wanted to continue their agitations. They wanted to have sabotage in our mines, in our transportation systems and throughout our industries. They did not have a solution of our problem in their hearts.
I would be the last to say that the labouring people of this country are receiving the remuneration they should receive; that they are living and working under first class conditions. However, I maintain that our problems, especially our labour problems, will never be solved by these agitators in the pay of a foreign institution. I feel free to speak of this. I maintain that this country has no right to try to impose its political beliefs upon any other country; yet communist Russia has tried to spread its beliefs throughout every section of the civilized world. I intend

Validity of Quebec Statute

to employ all my energy and limited talents in the fight against this curse which has been undermining the population in certain sections of our dominion and has also tried to undermine our institutions.
Perhaps you will ask what this has to with the padlock law in Quebec. I know something of that province because I was bom there. While I owe my primary loyalty to Ontario, my forefathers for the last four centuries are sleeping their last sleep in the Laurentian hills in the riding of Charlevoix. I know the make-up and mentality of the people of Quebec. I know their fine traditions. I know it will be surprising to many people in Quebec to know there are a few sections in that province, especially in the city of Montreal, where communism seems to have found a fertile field.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, I now wish to direct my remarks more particularly to my compatriots from the province of Quebec, in order to tell them that many young French Canadians-fine specimens of manhood, and intelligent young men-have played the part of assistant communist leaders during the strikes that have taken place in the forests of northern Ontario and in our mines. Speaking in the house on February 4, seven days later, the Minister of Justice complained as to criticisms leveled at him because he had not dealt with the padlock legislation. He said it was unfair to ask him for a decision so soon, because he had had the petition before him for only a few days. But he prepared the report on the Alberta acts the day they were received in Ottawa. He prepared. that report and recommended disallowance without a petition. May I point out that he had the padlock law before him from July 8 until January 28, when the petition was presented for disallowance or reference to the supreme court.
Here is a comparison in reference to a serious matter about which we should have
some explanation. It took less than one day's consideration for the minister to recommend disallowance of the Alberta acts-just one day for the government to call for a reference before the supreme court. Only eleven days intervened between assent and disallowance of the Alberta acts, whereas with respect to the "padlock" law, fourteen months have passed since assent, and the minister promised that a reference to the supreme court would have his serious consideration.
I do not like to reflect on the phrase "serious consideration", but the lapse of time in the present instance is an added justification for the smile which comes to people's faces when "serious consideration" is mentioned. More than eight months have elapsed since the first request for disallowance, four months since the first formal petition and two months since hearing counsel in support of the petition. I do not think the minister can say we have been impatient; any more patience in the matter and it could surely be said that patience had ceased to be a virtue.
I have a great many resolutions before me asking either for disallowance or for a reference to the supreme court. As the minister has probably had more than I have had, I shall not take the trouble to read them to the house. May I conclude with only one or two further observations, which I make as seriously, sincerely and as kindly as possible. There are many reasons why the "padlock" law should be either disallowed or referred to the supreme court for a decision as to validity. These reasons have been explained time and again. There is one reason, however, which I believe should weigh heavily with this government. It claims it is anxious that the unity of the Canadian people be maintained. We are all anxious that national unity should be strengthened, but I say in all earnestness that unity in Canada cannot be maintained if one province is going to be treated differently from another.

Mr. Speaker, I feel it my inescapable moral and legal duty to join in the protest which has been made by some hon. members against this legislation. I regard it as an awful invasion of the age-old liberties which we of the Anglo-Saxon race have always referred to with justifiable pride and reverence. These liberties have been won as the result of a thousand years of struggle, and in my judgment they have been violated by this legislation, Those thousand years of struggle were marked by considerable personal sacrifice and risk on the part of those who won them for
Validity of Quebec Statute

us. We are the recipients and heirs of the results of those efforts and we are also the guardians for the future. We must pass on to those who come after us these liberties sound and intact.
It seems incredible that in the year 1938 it is possible that there should be upon the statute 'books of one of our great provinces a law that permits the encroachment upon and the setting aside of what we have always regarded as the elementary rights of ordinary citizens. Here is what is possible under this legislation. An executive officer is enabled to punish a man iby padlocking his house before a court has found him guilty. The burden of proof of innocence is placed upon the person thus attacked, and there is no appeal from the decision of a single judge of the superior court. Any peace officer is enabled to seize literature, not only of a communistic nature-the interpretation of what constitutes communism is left to the uncontrolled discretion of the party who pleases to decide the matter-but of any sort of literature tending to produce communism. I quote from the petition sent in from the. Canadian Civil Liberties Union:
This act violates fundamental principles of the Canadian constitution. The preamble to the British North America Act states that Canada is to have a "constitution similar in principle to that of Great Britain."	This
phrase is based on Quebec resolution No. 3, which speaks of following "the model of the British constitution." Elementary principles of British constitutional government are freedom of speech, of the press and of public meeting subject to the limitations of the criminal law; the right of a man to a fair trial in open court if charged with an offence; a presumption of innocence in the accused until he is proven guilty; and freedom of the home from arbitrary search and interference by executive officers acting without judicial warrant.
There can be no doubt that all of these principles have been violated by this act. It was with astonishment that I listened to an hon. member read a list of the books and periodicals which had been seized. The whole thing struck me as being absolutely ridiculous. It is almost unbelievable that the speeches of Lloyd George, the books of Charles Dickens and of Sidney and Beatrice Webb have been seized. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has often stated in this house that the way to stop subversive activities in this country is to remove the cause. Has it ever occurred to any hon. member that there may be very definite causes for what are loosely referred to as subversive activities? _ I should like to quote from an article which I read this morning in an Edmonton paper, the People's Weekly of

May 1938. The writer of this article is Mr. S. Lapedes, secretary and organizer of the United Garment Workers of America. He says:
* ^jlShty per cent of those gainfully employed m Quebec receive wages lower than the minimum required for a decent standard of existence. In a parish near Quebec city a firm employs seventy-five workers at a maximum wage of eight cents an hour and a minimum of five cents. The minimum wage in Quebec is forty per cent lower than in Ontario.

I have heard the Minister of Justice repeatedly make the statement in this house that the way to correct subversive activities is to remove the cause. It is our business to see that these inhumanities are removed. I cannot describe this legislation as other than frantic, hysterical and altogether outrageous. It is just another melancholy example of the utter and complete bankruptcy of ideas which characterizes present day government and leadership. The attempt is made to treat the symptom rather than the disease. The attempt is made to rearrange the consequences rather than to discover and remove the causes. I have said ov er and over in the house that the resources of labour and material in this country are capable of producing an abundant and happy living for all our citizens, provided we use sound, scientific principles of production and distribution. Yet we are clinging to the carcasses of a dead system and a dead policy.
_ I appeal to my French-Canadian colleagues in the house. Over a period of centuries old France has produced a great number of brilliant and courageous defenders of democracy and freedom, and so has French Quebec. I shall not name them because they are well known to every hon. member. How does this legislation square with the immortal words of that great Frenchman who said:
I may disagree with everything you say, but I will defend with my life your right to say it.

Unemployed Men m Vancouver
I suggest that we should keep those words in mind and try to square our legislative enactments with them. May I suggest that we turn our attention to the urgent problem of preserving our political and industrial democracy here in new France? The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) suggested in the house about ten days ago that we should be prepared to endure "sore travail" in order to defend the democracy of old France. Let us get firmly established the industrial democracy of new France. Let us work on the principle that democracy, like charity, begins at home.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) has referred to the alacrity with which the government proceeded to disallow certain legislation when the interests of rich and powerful people in this country were in jeopardy or were questioned. One cannot help contrasting that with the fact that fourteen months have gone by, and we heard last night a recital of the terrible injustices and the serious invasions of the elementary principles of the rights of the people that have been going on in that province for fourteen months, and apparently no attention is paid thereto. This inaction on the part of the government raises a question which one hears being asked all over this country. Is there one law for the rich and another for the poor? I am reminded of the satirical remark made by another illustrious Frenchman, Anatole France. He said in one of his books:
The law in its majesty equally forbids the rich as well as the poor to sleep under bridges and steal bread.
It may be, and I believe it has been argued that the government should not exercise its powers of disallowance until an application seeking such action has been presented to it. But, I suggest, in the case of such gross, flagrant and palpable transgression of the elementary rights of private citizens the government should be empowered to act without unreasonable delay.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER-RESPONSIBILITY ATTACHING TO HOLDERS OF NATURALIZATION CERTIFICATES
speechtext:
Before the house resolves itself into committee of supply, I desire to direct attention to a few matters which, I think, constitute grievances that the government should take early steps to remedy.
First, the public property of Canada is vested in the crown in right of the dominion. The post office property of Canada is vested
in the crown in right of the dominion, and
has been constructed by the taxpayers of Canada for public use.
Second, it is the duty of the government of Canada to see that the property owned by the Canadian people for Canadian purposes is available for the purposes for which it was provided.
Third, a post office is a public place under the provisions of the criminal code.
Fourth, during the last several days the entrance hall of the post office at Vancouver has been completely filled with large numbers of idle and unemployed persons. It may be true that there has been a failure on the part of the national government to take appropriate steps to provide for them. That, however, is entirely beside the question. It is not my purpose or intention to indulge in any discussion with respect to that matter, except to point out that there is a large measure of sympathy on the part of many citizens of Vancouver for those who thus find themselves unemployed.
Fifth, under the law of this country, when persons thus unemployed or persons who have nothing to do but loiter in a public place-* and under the code a post office is a public place-they are trespassers.
Sixth, the criminal code of this country has provided that it is the duty of the owner of property that is held, as a post office is, by the crown in right of the dominion, to remove with as much force as may be necessary those persons who are trespassing upon that property. Further, the criminal code has provided that in the event of trespassers resisting attempts to remove them, they are deemed to commit an assault without justification or provocation. That is section 61 of the Canadian criminal code.
I should like you Mr. Speaker, to realize that this country is now being held up before the world as a country in which there is no longer respect for law and order. Blazoned upon the headlines of great journals throughout the American continent is the statement that sit-down strikes are now the order of the day in Canada, and that the public property held by the crown in right of this dominion, not of the province, is no longer available for the purposes for which it has been constructed, but that men by hundreds are sitting there, not for hours but for days. I have no suggestion to make as to the solution of the difficulty between these individuals and the crown as represented by either the province or the dominion, by the government of the one or the other, but as a

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
Canadian I protest against the continuance of public property being held by those who are trespassing upon it. I feel quite certain that if this matter were put before them as it should be, and they were asked to leave this property at once, as trespassers, this would have the desired result; for these men are not ignorant men. The evidence of the press indicates that, in many instances, they are men of education, understanding and appreciation, and yet to enforce their demands they are carrying on a sit-down strike in the post office at Vancouver. Last year the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) declared in this house in bold terms, as reported at page 2114 of Hansard, that sit-down strikes should not be tolerated in Canada. It is true that what he had reference to at that particular time were sit-down strikes in industrial and commercial properties; but whatever may be said with respect to sit-down strikes in commercial and industrial properties, however much you may declare and inveigh against them, you must realize that a sit-down strike by those who are trespassers upon public property is one of the most serious things that could happen in this dominion.
The press in Vancouver has been directing attention to this matter. As I say, it is now being blazoned in the public press of other countries. I ask the administration to take immediate steps, on behalf of the Canadian people, to vindicate the majesty and authority of the law and see to it that those who trespass upon public property in defiance of the laws of the country are requested peaceably, honourably and fairly to leave the public property upon which they are trespassers; failing which, the steps provided for by the criminal code should be taken without delay. It is that, Mr. Speaker, to which I wish to direct the attention of the house at this time. It is a real grievance which does not affect the community of Vancouver alone. It is a grievance that affects every Canadian, whoever he may be, who is interested in the fair name and fame of this dominion and has any respect for its reputation among the peoples of the world.
I now direct attention to the second grievance about which, I think, the people of this country are greatly concerned. I hold in my hand what I dare say has been seen by many people, namely, a statement made by a returned Italian named Vincent Scap-patura, in the North Bay Nugget on May 27, 1938, couched in terms which I think the right hon. the Minister of Justice will admit should not be permitted to be used by any man who is a naturalized British subject in Canada, in which statement he refers

to our institutions as being so lacking in vigour and strength as compared with the institutions that have been set up in Italy; that England had to back down; that Mussolini "just wont scare"; that when the British fleet was concentrated in the Mediterranean, Mussolini could have sunk it, and that the British navy was too weak and unorganized to do anything about it. And so far as Canada is concerned, he points out that Canada cannot do certain things in connection with certain matters with which we deal every day, because in this democracy we are unequal to it and the only way in which we-can deal with these matters is through the-application of certain principles. To quote the words attributed to him:
"When there was a lack of employment among farm workers, the fascists sent agents to survey the farms," related Mr. Scappatura. "Work and repairs that were needed were advised to be done. Not next week or when the farmer felt like it but now!"
And then he goes on to point to the regulations that are applied with reference to the life of the farmers and others in Italy. I am not going to take up the time of the house reading it, but there are nine proposals which he asserted in this country and which are not only a reflection upon this dominion but a reflection upon the British crown and upon British public men as well as upon our institutions and our form of government. This man is a naturalized Canadian. He has been absent from this country for several years, and he came back the other day. He says that he is going to get a passport to go back to Italy; that he will sell out his property there and then come back to this country.
I ask the government of the day to enforce the provisions of the statute which was placed upon the statute books by common consent-not by a party measure. I refer to the Naturalization Act, being chapter 138 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, the first subsection of section 9, which reads as follows:	[DOT]
Where the governor in council, upon the report of the minister, is satisfied that a certificate of naturalization granted by the minister under this act or granted under anj' Naturalization Act heretofore in force in Canada has been obtained by false representation or fraud, or by concealment of material circumstances, or that the person to whom the certificate was granted has shown himself by act or speech to be disaffected or disloyal to His Majesty, the governor in council shall by order revoke the certificate.

Yes; that was what I was about to say in my next sentence. It is very frequently done, and I hope that as long as we have a country it will continue to be done on appropriate occasions, as I believe it will be by all governments and under all circumstances. I direct public attention to this matter rather than the attention of the Minister of Justice personally, in the first instance, because I think it is of the utmost importance that it should be known by those who have come to this country, who have made their homes here, who 'have secured naturalization certificates, who have received the benefits and advantages of our institutions, that it is to their advantage to realize that they must conduct themselves as citizens of this new country and not as citizens of the old. I know that the Minister of Justice not only holds that view but has had occasion frequently, very frequently, to exercise the power that is involved in the cancellation of certificates; and my grievance-I put it frankly, not on my own behalf-is that such a statement as I shall hand to the minister should be made by any man in this country and that he should come back to Canada after an absence and declare that he is going to get a passport for the purpose I have indicated. I shall not, of course, make any pronouncement as to . the authenticity or otherwise of the statements that appear in the public press. I saw them in the press and debated with myself as to what my duty was in the premises. I think, having regard to the troubled times in which we live, it is highly important that those who obtain naturalization certificates in Canada should realize that these certificates may for just reason and cause be cancelled. I was told only a few hays ago that if that were generally understood by some in this country, we would have less occasion for worry in connection with [DOT]certain types of unrest which manifest themselves in one or two sections of Canada.
These are the two matters to which I direct the attention of the government at this time before we go into supply, in order that the government may have timely notice of a situation which later undoubtedly will engage this house in debate. I have endeavoured not to make any statement that is controversial in the sense of not being strictly within the terms of the information which is in my possesion. Had I read from the public press *of Vancouver some of the statements which
have appeared there, the statement that I have made would be much stronger than it now is. I do believe, however, that one of the best methods by which we can deal with this whole situation-the last one to which I have referred-is for an authoritative statement to be made at the appropriate time by the Minister of Justice as to the liability and responsibility attaching to those who have obtained naturalization certificates in this country through their residence and through their oath of allegiance which is, of course, a condition precedent to the certificates being issued under our statute.
