maintopic: CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER-RESPONSIBILITY ATTACHING TO HOLDERS OF NATURALIZATION CERTIFICATES
speechtext: I should like to say a few words as a citizen of Vancouver, stressing more particularly the necessity for the government to do something

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
to place these men at work. That is a responsibility from which the government cannot escape. These men are single unemployed transients. I believe several thousand of the men of that class now in Vancouver do not even belong to British Columbia; they are men from the other provinces of Canada. The stand taken by this government and the provincial government is that they will ship back to their respective provinces those men who do not belong to British Columbia. But the difficulty is that when these men get back to their home provinces they are treated there as transients; they cannot establish any claim to relief, and so naturally enough they will not go. The men are not criminals in any sense of the word, although I think they are being wrongly led. Quite apart from the men who are in the post office and the art gallery, there have been some going out during the last week begging for money, shaking little tin cans before the citizens, whereupon the city police pick them up on a charge of obstructing the police. The reason that charge is laid is that it is an indictable offence and therefore the province has to pay for their keep. Actually they are not obstructing the police at all; they hop into the police wagon and go off with smiles on their faces.
That is the position in my city, and the sad part is that it is breaking down the spirit of the citizens, breaking the morale of the city. It is something they see every day, talk about every day; it is right there on their doorstep. The result is that business is slowed down; there is no chance for more jobs in the city; it will simply mean that there will be more unemployed. I suggest to the government that the main reason why this problem is not being dealt with, was not dealt with last week, is because Ottawa is 3,000 miles away from Vancouver; our people are out there over the mountains on the Pacific slope, out of touch, and the government here does not realize how serious this question is for the people of Vancouver. If the same situation existed in Toronto, with three times the population of Vancouver, you would have
15.000	single transient unemployed there, and you would have 3,000 men camped in the Toronto post office and the Royal Ontario museum. No one in this house can tell me that if that state of affairs existed, the government here would not have taken action a long time ago. If it were in Montreal, you would have 20,000 single unemployed, and
4.000	of these men parked in the post office there and the art gallery. Then the members of the government here would realize the seriousness of the situation.
I suggest to the government that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) should go to the coast at once, where he could see the situation for himself. I suggest also that some of the forestry camps be reopened until it is possible to give these men work on the works projects. Almost a month ago I told the minister this trouble was coming, and as I pointed out then, these men have been kept all. winter in forestry camps; they are not like the men on the prairies or in Ontario who have been kept on the farms, and can go on with farm work in the summer. These men have been in the forestry camps, which are closed each spring. The men are turned loose, and they all drift to the one city. That is how the trouble came about. We have had the same thing each year for the last two or three years, and I submit to the ministers who are here to-night that some action should be taken at once. I am not saying anything about using force, but I place emphasis on the need for giving these young men work. If you do that, there will be no trouble at all about getting them out of the post office and the art gallery.

Mr. Speaker, we are a long way from Vancouver, and in a matter of this kind I would far sooner let the officials of the government in that city look after matters than try to deal with the difficulty at such long range. So far as I know, and I think so far as the government have been informed, the men about whom we are speaking this evening have been fairly well behaved under the circumstances. They are not in exactly a normal frame of mind in a great many instances. If they had desired to do harm in that city, they were in an art gallery, where they could have done incalculable damage in a very short space of time, but the fact that they have kept discipline there and do not want to damage property at least speaks well for the behaviour of the men involved. It may sound almost humourous to think that on crown property these men were almost guilty of having a pleasant evening. Well, Mr. Speaker, I would far sooner find the men doing that and behaving with a sense of decency than attempt to remove them by force and possibly have them barricade themselves in these public buildings. Instead of condemning the government for the action they have taken, I think there is some commendation due them, particularly those officials in charge in Vancouver, for the patience that has been shown under the circumstances. Further, I think the people of

Unemployed, Men in Vancouver
Vancouver have shown a great deal of sympathy and have given a great deal of support to the men involved.
When a moment ago I said they were not entirely normal I meant that they were not leading entirely normal lives. For several months previously they were in camps in the country. Then they came to the city and found no one willing to assume responsibility for their maintenance or even to help them obtain work. I would suggest, following the last speaker, that the government should exert every possible endeavour to see that these men are given a guarantee of some kind in regard to food, clothing and shelter, and then they should be provided with work. I think, if they were given some assurance of work in the near future, the trouble in regard to these men would soon be ended.

Mr. Mr. Speaker, this is Canada, and day by day we are looking at and hearing about a most extraordinary state of affairs that exists in the Vancouver post office. I cannot listen to these stories without my mind going back again and again to the situation with which the late administration had to deal at a time when depression was much worse and unemployment far more widespread. At that time the government of the day had to handle matters as they found them, and in devising methods to meet the situation with which they were confronted the government met with nothing but remonstrance, criticism and obstacles on the part of the opposition of that day. I remember the methods employed by the late administration to deal with that portion of this problem which fell to the dominion through agreement with the provinces, that is. the care of the single, homeless unemployed; methods which gave satisfaction to a very considerable number of those men, who were glad to receive shelter from the storm and subsistence, and to do work which was laid out for them. But everything that was done by the late administration for this class of men was condemned and ridiculed by those then opposed to us.
How has the problem changed? Those camps were closed. It is true that some of the camps have been reopened by other organizations for this purpose. When the camps were closed, the numbers in them having been greatly reduced, an arrangement was made between the present government and the two railway companies to employ these men for a certain length of time. When we endeavoured to get information at the end of that period as to what had become of the men who had been in the camps, we found it extremely

difficult to find any trace of them. But they have turned up since in the persons of these single, homeless, unemployed still not dealt with by the dominion government. So we look on the situation in that province to the west, which has always had the most difficult part of this problem to look after, and which has had to handle it largely by itself, and we see a condition of affairs the news value of which is being exploited by the press of the world, with the result that the people of the world are smiling at Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to tender any advice to the government on how to deal with this problem. There is only one angle of it that I propose to mention, and it is the manner in which we have educated numbers of our single men in this country in the idea that if they fail to find jobs for themselves, a generous government will turn in and provide them with a home, with food to eat and with raiment to wear. To my way of thinking that is one of the greatest injuries we have done to the young men of this country; we have robbed them of their initiative, destroyed their ambition to go out and find work, to do any job they can find. I am afraid it is only too true that once a young man works on a government job it is very hard to get him to work for a farmer or a contractor. If he gets work with the government one year, working eight hours a day and not being pushed too hard, he wants that job the next year, and if he does not get it then it is going to be just too bad for all concerned.
My suggestion is that some way be found of getting our young people away from this idea that they must eternally depend on some governing body to look after them. As I understand it, these young men in British Columbia were offered transportation back to their home provinces. They were taken into those camps under the youth training scheme, given employment during a time of stress, and then had the chance to go back to their own provinces where very likely they would have been able to find some kind of work.
Where is the work?

I venture to say that many of these men, at all events, could find work on the farms of the different provinces if they wanted to; but that is the trouble; you cannot get them to take that work after they have been doing government jobs. They do not want that kind of work.

Are there any unemployed in the other provinces?

Sup-ply-Post Office
Not in the rural districts. There are plenty of farmers looking for men.
Is the fault that of the men who are in the post office and art gallery of Vancouver, or is it the fault of this nation which has not been able to meet their needs for work?

I think it is greatly the fault of the young men there, that they did not get out of Vancouver when they had the money and the price to get out where work was to be found, and to. take on the work available.
Does that clear us of our responsibility?

I do not see why any
governing body should have to take the responsibility for taking care of all of its citizens. If we are going to adopt that sort of attitude-well, what are we drifting to?-just a dictatorship; that is all.

Is the hon. member aware that a large number of young men are from the drought areas and could not return to the conditions which obtained there without being a great burden upon those municipalities.

I suppose they are putting in crops in the dried-out areas this year, and in doing that they require help. If they have moisture, they will naturally want to put in crops, and in doing that there would be employment for numbers of these men.

The hon. member says that he supposes; is there any indication that a person would get employment if he arrived there? You cannot go to the prairie provinces only on a presumption.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY TABLING OF NEW PROPOSALS FOR DEVELOPMENT OF GREAT LAKES SYSTEM
speechtext: On May 28, the Secretary of State of the United States addressed a note to the Canadian Minister at Washington setting forth new proposals for the development of the great lakes-St. Lawrence system for navigation and power. That note was accompanied by a draft treaty, and the government of the United States, we are informed, desires to publish this to-morrow. So it is only fair to the house that I should lay on the table four copies of both the note of the United States Secretary of State and the proposed draft treaty. Of course we have not considered it yet.
